summary: For children aged 8–9, mathematical modelling of multiplicative situations (area/array, recipe-scaling with fractions, unit conversion) must complete the full cycle: choose a representation that exposes the multiplicative STRUCTURE, run the calculation, and then take the 'return trip' — read the number back into the situation with its unit and referent attached ('375 g of flour', not a bare '375'). The hardest interpret-back at this age is the fractional one: 3/4 of 500 g is a quantity of a real ingredient, not a bare fraction. Each of the three situations ends in the same interpret-back gate. Guidance centres on a hands-on interactive build where the model and equation are two views of one structure, supported by an in-role client conversation, a labelled primer, and sub-skill checks.
misconceptions: Stops at the bare number and never re-attaches the unit or meaning ('375') so cannot say what was found
Treats 3/4 of 500 as a fraction answer rather than a quantity of grams of a real ingredient
Reaches for a keyword ('of means times', 'altogether means add') instead of modelling the situation, so mis-sets the operation
Applies a memorised conversion rule (×100) without a structure to check it against, so an inverted conversion (cm to m by ×100) goes unnoticed

activities.title: Tile a floor, scale a recipe, convert a length — then say what the number means
steps: Drag square tiles into a rectangle to build an array; watch the matching equation form alongside (e.g. 6 rows × 4 = 24) so the picture and the equation are two views of one structure
Compute the result, then complete a compulsory interpret-back step: state or type the answer WITH its unit and what it refers to ('24 tiles', '375 g of flour'), not just the digits
Carry a result back into a real decision: if tiles come 10 to a box, work out that 24 tiles needs 3 boxes and that 2 boxes (only 20 tiles) would leave you short
Repeat the same shape with a recipe bar: cut a bar of 500 g into quarters and take 3/4 to get '375 g of flour'

Repeat with a metres-to-centimetres double number line (scaling ladder): read one scale against the other, then complete the same interpret-back gate by stating the converted length with its unit and referent (e.g. '3 m is 300 cm')

At least once, meet a problem where a surface keyword ('altogether', 'of', 'times') points to the wrong operation; use numberless/number-later framing and set the operation from the structure of the situation instead
activities.insight: A model is not finished until the number is re-clothed in context: every answer needs its unit and referent, and should be sense-checked against the situation. The array/area picture IS the multiplication (rows × columns = product; l × w = area), and scaling and conversion share a multiplicative, proportional structure.

activities.title: Convince the client: 375 of what?
steps: Work with an in-role client — a baker scaling a recipe, or a decorator ordering tiles — who needs a real answer for a real order
State the result in words with its unit and referent, and justify that the quantity is reasonable for the real order
Respond when the client pushes back ('you said 375 — 375 of what?') by naming the unit and checking the amount makes sense
Decide the practical consequence: how many boxes to buy, how much flour to measure
activities.insight: Voicing and defending the interpret-back — naming the unit, the referent, and a reasonableness check — is the reflective half of the modelling cycle. The number only means something when tied back to the real decision it informs.

activities.title: Primer: the array beside the equation
steps: Explore a labelled array or bar where taps reveal the parts: 'this side = number of rows', 'the area = the product = the number of tiles'
Connect each labelled part of the picture to the matching part of the written multiplication or fraction sentence
activities.insight: Rows × columns IS the product and area IS l × w: the picture and the equation are two views of one multiplicative structure.

activities.title: Sub-skill checks: product and converted length
steps: Check a computed product from a given array (rows × columns)
Check a converted length (e.g. metres to centimetres) for a given structure
activities.insight: The underlying arithmetic sub-skills (finding a product, carrying out a conversion) must be reliable so attention is free for the modelling and interpret-back.

checkQuestion: A recipe for 4 people uses 500 g of flour. You want to make it for 6 people. A friend works out 500 ÷ 4 × 6 and says '750'. Is the recipe finished being solved? Talk me through what 750 means and whether you'd trust it.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child treating '750' as unfinished until it is read back into the situation as '750 grams of flour for 6 people', and sense-checking it (6 people is 1.5× as many as 4, so a bit more than 500 g is expected; 750 fits). A child who says only 'the answer is 750' or 'it's 750 people/cups' has done the arithmetic but not the modelling.
